Test and draw the association of two categorical variables

Source: R/mosaic_analysis.R
mosaic_analysis.Rd

mosaic_analysis() tests the association between two categorical columns of a data frame and draws it as a mosaic. It builds their contingency table, drops sparse categories (fewer than min_count rows), runs a Pearson chi-square test (or Fisher's exact test), computes Cramer's V with an effect-size label, and draws a flat ggplot2 mosaic in which tile area is the cell count and the fill is the cell's standardised residual. The per-cell results come as a data frame, one row per cell.

The p-value tests the null hypothesis that the two variables are independent; with large samples almost any departure is significant, so read Cramer's V for the size of the association. The label follows Cohen's (1988) thresholds for the table's degrees of freedom, min(rows, columns) - 1: 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.50 for small / medium / large at 1, 0.07 / 0.21 / 0.35 at 2, 0.06 / 0.17 / 0.29 at 3, and 0.05 / 0.15 / 0.25 above (Cohen's w divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom); a V below the small threshold is labelled "negligible". The residuals are chisq.test()'s standardised residuals, roughly standard normal under independence, so one beyond about +-2 marks a cell that holds more (or fewer) rows than independence predicts; with many cells, some pass that line by chance.

Usage

mosaic_analysis(
  data,
  var1,
  var2,
  min_count = 10L,
  test = c("chisq", "fisher"),
  percentage_base = c("total", "row", "column"),
  tile_label = c("count", "percent", "residual", "category", "none"),
  title = "",
  ...,
  nested = FALSE,
  nested_method = c("rao_scott", "donner_klar", "cmh", "gee", "glmm"),
  actor = NULL,
  report = FALSE
)

# S3 method for class 'mosaic_analysis'
plot(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mosaic_analysis'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mosaic_analysis'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame holding the two variables. Rows missing either of them (or an actor column) are left out; a var1 or var2 that is not a column of data, or no complete rows, raises an error.

var1

The name of the first variable, drawn as the mosaic's columns (column width is its marginal share).

var2

The name of the second variable, stacked within each column.

min_count

The smallest number of rows a category must have to be kept. Categories of either variable with fewer rows in the full table are dropped, in one pass, before the test. Default 10. If fewer than two categories of either variable remain, an error is raised.

test

The test reported: "chisq" (default) for Pearson's chi-square test, or "fisher" for Fisher's exact test: exact for a 2 x 2 table, and otherwise with a p-value simulated from 10,000 tables (so it changes with the random seed and cannot fall below 1/10,001). Cramer's V and the residuals come from Pearson's chi-square (V from the statistic without Yates' correction). Used when nested = FALSE; given with nested = TRUE it is ignored with a warning of class nestimate_ignored_argument.

percentage_base

What the pct column and the "percent" tile label are a percentage of: "total" (default) the whole table, "row" each level of var1, "column" each level of var2.

tile_label

What to print inside each tile: "count" (default), "percent", "residual", "category" (the var2 level) or "none".

title

The plot title. Default "" (none).

...

Further styling for the flat mosaic:

  • labels: col_label_side, row_label_side, col_label_angle, row_label_angle, label_size, min_label_h and min_label_w;

  • legend: show_legend, legend_position, legend_size and legend_title;

  • fill: range and palette (default the ColorBrewer RdBu ramp);

  • pct_base, which overrides percentage_base in the plot only.

Column labels turn vertical when there are more than 6 columns; col_label_angle sets an angle. Any other name raises an error. For the plot() method: the same styling and title, overriding what the fit stored; for the print() and summary() methods: ignored.

nested

Whether the rows are nested in actors and the test should allow for it. Default FALSE: every row is independent, as before. TRUE reports nested_method and needs actor; see Nested data.

nested_method

With nested = TRUE, the test: "rao_scott" (default), "donner_klar", "cmh", "gee" or "glmm". A test that cannot run on the design raises nestimate_bad_input; "glmm" needs the lme4 package.

actor

With nested = TRUE (required then): the name of the column whose values identify the actors, or several names for nested levels, outermost first (e.g. c("Group", "Actor")). nested_method and actor given with nested = FALSE are ignored with a warning of class nestimate_ignored_argument.

report

Whether to report the test: TRUE draws it as the plot subtitle and prints it as a one-row data frame with the columns of mosaic_test() but note. Default FALSE. The test is always in the stats table and in print().

x

For the plot() and print() methods: a mosaic_analysis.

object

For the summary() method: a mosaic_analysis.

Value

A mosaic_analysis object. print() shows the sample size, the test, Cramer's V with its label and the dropped categories, and returns the object invisibly; summary() returns the per-cell data frame (the counts table below) with the one-row test summary attached as the attribute "stats"; plot() draws the mosaic on the active device, with new styling if given, and returns the ggplot invisibly. The object is a list with:

plot

The flat mosaic, a ggplot. Building the object does not draw it.

counts

A data frame with one row per (var1, var2) cell: the two variables (named after them), observed, expected, residual (the standardised residual, or the nested test's residual, NA where it is undefined and drawn at 0) and pct (on percentage_base); expected and residual are rounded to 3 decimals, pct to 2.

stats

A one-row data frame: test, statistic, df, df2, p_value, cramers_v, effect_size, n, clusters, design_effect and icc, rounded (statistic and cramers_v to 3 decimals, p_value to 4 significant digits). statistic and df are NA for Fisher's test. df2 (the denominator degrees of freedom of the Rao-Scott F), clusters, design_effect and icc are NA where the test has none.

test

The htest object of the test reported; NULL for a nested test.

actor

The actor column names, or NULL.

cramers_v, effect_size

Cramer's V, unrounded, and its label. V is computed from Pearson's chi-square without Yates' continuity correction, as Cramer defined it, so a perfect 2 x 2 association gives 1; the 2 x 2 test reported keeps the correction.

table

The filtered contingency table.

removed

The dropped categories, as a list with var1 and var2.

n_original, n_filtered

The number of complete rows before and after the sparse categories are dropped.

vars

The two variable names, as c(var1 = , var2 = ).

plot_parts, plot_args

The residual matrix, the table, the test line drawn as the subtitle with report = TRUE, and the styling, kept so plot() can redraw without testing again.

Nested data

Pearson's test treats every row as an independent observation. When rows are nested in actors (events within students, students within classes), rows of one actor resemble each other and the test is too liberal. Set nested = TRUE and name the actor column(s) in actor (as in permutation()). The test is then nested_method, one of five that allow for the nesting; each gives a test and its own residual per cell, which fills the mosaic.

"rao_scott" (default)

Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-square, reported as an F statistic on fractional degrees of freedom (the default of survey::svychisq(), which it reproduces for an unweighted cluster sample). Works for any cluster sizes and when both variables vary within clusters. design_effect is the mean generalised design effect; 1 means the clustering costs nothing. Residual: the standardised residual divided by the square root of the cell's design effect (cluster-robust over simple-random-sampling variance of p_ij - p_i. p_.j); with one row per cluster it is chisq.test()'s, and it is NA where the cell's design effect is zero. With empty cells the design effects are those of the estimable contrasts. The test is liberal with few actors when one variable is constant within actors: in simulations of 3 x 4 tables its type I error at alpha = 0.05 was 0.22 with 10 actors, 0.10 with 30 and 0.06 with 100.

"donner_klar"

Pearson's chi-square divided, group by group, by the inflation factor 1 + (m - 1) * rho (its weighted form for unequal cluster sizes), where rho is the ANOVA intracluster correlation of var2, pooled within the levels of the other variable. For designs where one variable is constant within each cluster, as in a cluster-randomised trial; otherwise an error is raised. icc is rho; a negative estimate is reported and used as 0. Residual: the standardised residual divided by the square root of its group's factor.

"cmh"

Generalised Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test with each cluster as a stratum: is there an association within clusters? Suits a few clusters with enough rows each; both variables must vary within clusters, and clusters with fewer than two rows are left out (clusters counts those that inform the test). Residual: summed observed minus expected over the square root of the summed hypergeometric variances. This tests conditional association, whereas Rao-Scott and GEE test marginal association; the null hypotheses can differ. Stratification does not correct arbitrary serial dependence among observations within an actor.

"gee"

Marginal model for var2 given var1 with an identity link and independence working correlation; Wald chi-square with the cluster-robust (sandwich) covariance for equal distributions of var2 across var1, on (rows - 1) (columns - 1) degrees of freedom. When the covariance has lower rank (fewer actors than degrees of freedom, or cells that never occur) the test would depend on the order of rows and columns, and an error of class nestimate_bad_input is raised. The Wald test is liberal unless the actors are many relative to the degrees of freedom: in simulations of 3 x 4 tables its type I error at alpha = 0.05 was 0.28 with 30 actors and 0.11 with 100. Residual: the share of var2 within the level of var1 minus the pooled share, over its cluster-robust standard error.

"glmm"

Log-linear Poisson mixed model of the cluster-by-cell counts with random intercepts for cluster-by-var1 and cluster-by-var2 at every level of actor, so several columns give nested random effects (outermost first); Wald chi-square on the interaction. Fitted by lme4::glmer(nAGQ = 0), a faster, less exact approximation than the default Laplace fit; needs lme4, and a failed fit raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input. With an empty cell the Wald test loses power (its interaction term runs to minus infinity). Residual: observed minus expected count under independence, over its cluster-robust standard error (the GLMM supplies the test, the residual is model-free). With several actor levels, this standard error clusters at the outermost level; it is undefined with fewer than two outer actors. With about 10 actors this standard error is small and 7 to 8% of null cells pass 1.96.

With several actor columns, the four other tests use the outermost (the first), which carries the dependence of every level below it. Cramer's V is the pooled-table effect size whatever the test: the clustering changes the uncertainty, not the size of the association.

Methods

  • plot.mosaic_analysis() redraws the flat mosaic from the stored contingency table and residuals, so the styling can change without the test being run again. Any flat-mosaic styling argument (tile_label, pct_base, col_label_side, legend_size, ...) can be overridden through ....

References

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Rao, J. N. K., & Scott, A. J. (1984). On chi-squared tests for multiway contingency tables with cell proportions estimated from survey data. The Annals of Statistics, 12(1), 46–60. doi:10.1214/aos/1176346391

Donner, A., & Klar, N. (1994). Methods for comparing event rates in intervention studies when the unit of allocation is a cluster. American Journal of Epidemiology, 140(3), 279–289. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a117247

Landis, J. R., Heyman, E. R., & Koch, G. G. (1978). Average partial association in three-way contingency tables: A review and discussion of alternative tests. International Statistical Review, 46(3), 237–254. doi:10.2307/1402373

Liang, K.-Y., & Zeger, S. L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73(1), 13–22. doi:10.1093/biomet/73.1.13

Agresti, A. (2013). Categorical data analysis (3rd ed.), chapter 13. Wiley.

See also

mosaic_plot for the network/table mosaic (which also accepts style = "flat"); mosaic_test for every test, clustered or not, side by side in one table.

Examples

data(group_regulation_long, package = "Nestimate")
res <- mosaic_analysis(group_regulation_long, "Course", "Action",
                       min_count = 20)
res
#> Mosaic analysis: Course x Action
#>   N = 27533 (filtered from 27533); table 3 x 9
#>   Chi-square: X2 = 233.560, df = 16, p < 2.2e-16
#>   Cramer's V = 0.065 (negligible)
head(summary(res))
#>   Course   Action observed expected residual  pct
#> 1      A    adapt      140  249.303   -9.430 0.51
#> 2      B    adapt      261  193.688    6.059 0.95
#> 3      C    adapt      153  111.009    4.502 0.56
#> 4      A cohesion      923  827.560    4.631 3.35
#> 5      B cohesion      590  642.945   -2.680 2.14
#> 6      C cohesion      326  368.495   -2.563 1.18
# \donttest{
plot(res, tile_label = "percent")


# Actions are nested in students: Rao-Scott test by student
nested <- mosaic_analysis(group_regulation_long, "Course", "Action",
                          nested = TRUE, actor = "Actor")
nested
#> Mosaic analysis: Course x Action
#>   N = 27533 (filtered from 27533); table 3 x 9
#>   Rao-Scott: F(13.45, 26887.5) = 14.99, p < 1e-16; 2000 actors, design effect 0.97
#>   Actor: Actor
#>   Cramer's V = 0.065 (negligible)
# }
